section_summaries.epidemiology: Yellow fever (YF) is a mosquito-borne viral disease endemic to sub-Saharan Africa and tropical South America, estimated to cause 200,000 disease cases and 30,000 deaths annually. Cases are primarily reported among men with occupational exposures in forested areas in South America. In Africa, annual cases vary substantially due to recognition and reporting variations, ranging from 1 to 5000 cases. The disease's natural occurrence can fluctuate, with recent re-appearances in Angola (2016) and coastal Brazil (2017). Delineation of affected areas relies on surveillance for animal reservoirs and vectors, accurate diagnosis, and prompt reporting of human cases.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: YF virus is a positive-sense RNA flavivirus (family Flaviviridae) antigenically related to dengue, Zika, West Nile, St. Louis encephalitis, and Japanese encephalitis viruses. It has three transmission cycles: jungle (nonhuman primates and tree-hole mosquitoes like Aedes or Haemagogus spp.), savannah (tree-hole Aedes spp. between humans and animals/humans), and urban (humans and urban mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti). Infected humans develop peak viremia, infectious to mosquitoes shortly before and 3-5 days after fever onset. Direct person-to-person transmission of YF virus has not been documented, though perinatal transmission from an infected mother to infant at birth has been reported, and transmission might theoretically occur through blood transfusion, organ transplantation, intrauterine transmission, or breastfeeding.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Most YF virus infections are asymptomatic. For clinical disease, the incubation period is typically 3-9 days. Mild YF is a self-limited febrile illness with acute onset of fever and headache, sometimes accompanied by chills, myalgia, lumbosacral pain, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Faget's sign (relative bradycardia with elevated temperature) may be present. Viremia usually lasts about 3 days. Most patients recover uneventfully, but approximately 12% (range 5-26%) of infected persons develop a more severe form within 48 hours following the viremic period. Symptoms include fever, vomiting, epigastric pain, jaundice, renal insufficiency, cardiovascular instability, and a bleeding diathesis (hematemesis, melena, metrorrhagia, hematuria, petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis). Physical findings include scleral and dermal icterus, hemorrhages, and epigastric tenderness. Severe disease with hepatorenal dysfunction has a case-fatality ratio of 30-60%.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Laboratory findings in YF vary by severity and stage: leukopenia may occur in the first week, followed by leukocytosis in the second. Hyperbilirubinemia may be present early, peaking by the end of the first week. Elevated serum transaminase levels occur in hepatorenal disease and can persist for up to 2 months. Patients with hemorrhagic manifestations often have elevated prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, decreased platelet counts, and fibrin-split products. Diagnosis involves testing serum for viral RNA or virus-specific IgM and neutralizing antibodies. Virus or viral RNA is detectable by isolation or RT-PCR in serum during the first 3-4 days of illness, but should not be used for excluding the diagnosis due to potential absence later. Serologic cross-reactions with other flaviviruses (e.g., West Nile or dengue viruses) necessitate confirmation with specific tests like plaque-reduction neutralization. Immunohistochemical staining of formalin-fixed material can detect YF viral antigen in pathologic specimens. Health care providers should contact their state or local health department or national laboratories for assistance with diagnostic testing. Preliminary diagnosis is based on the patient's clinical features, YF vaccination status, and travel history. YF with jaundice must be differentiated from viral hepatitis, malaria, leptospirosis, Congo-Crimean hemorrhagic fever, Rift Valley fever, typhoid, Q fever, typhus, and drug/toxic causes of jaundice. Other viral hemorrhagic fevers typically without jaundice (dengue, Lassa, Marburg, Ebola, Bolivian, Argentinean, Venezuelan hemorrhagic fevers) are also differential diagnoses.
section_summaries.treatment: No specific anti-viral treatment exists for Yellow Fever; management is supportive, focusing on symptoms and the organ systems involved. Rest, fluids, and acetaminophen or paracetamol relieve milder fever and myalgia symptoms. Aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be avoided due to the risk for hemorrhagic complications. Although multiple drugs have been evaluated or empirically used, none has shown specific benefit.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention is critical to lower disease risk and mortality, involving vaccination and personal protective measures. Mosquito prevention includes using insect repellent, wearing permethrin-impregnated clothing, and staying in accommodations with screened or air-conditioned rooms. A live-attenuated YF vaccine is recommended for those ">="9 months of age traveling to or residing in YF-risk areas in South America and Africa. A single dose of YF vaccine is sufficient for most individuals to confer sustained lifelong protective immunity against YF disease. International health regulations allow countries to require proof of YF vaccination at least 10 days prior to entry; the certificate is valid for life. Common post-vaccination adverse events include fever, headache, myalgia, and injection site reactions. Rare but serious adverse events include immediate hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reactions, YF vaccine-associated neurologic disease, and YF vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease. Vaccination should only occur for persons at risk for exposure to YF virus or those requiring proof of vaccination, with contraindications and precautions observed.
